metadata.title: On weight initialization in deep neural networks

extraction_notes.note: Sections 2-3 are a running derivation with no result statements; the numbered equations are the nodes and the 'Using (x) ... yields (y)' prose is recorded as named uses edges between equations, not as proof nodes.
The label eq:tanh1 is defined twice (equations 14 and 16), so \ref{eq:tanh1} in the Figure 1 caption is ambiguous; \enum{} is the author's label-wrapping macro and stays in equation statements.
claim origin external vs paper: the paper re-derives v^2=2/N but attributes the result to He et al.; marked external with the derivation PP4 as paper.
remark or claim: a self-contained numeric aside explaining OpenP1; kept as remark (the author also swaps 22 and 30 layers in its last sentence).

metadata.extraction_comment: The propositions' proofs are run-in prose ending in \qedsymbol, not proof environments.

nodes.statement: The first systematic analysis of this problem was conducted by Glorot and Bengio who showed that for a linear activation function, the optimal value of v^2 = 1/N, where N is the number of nodes feeding into that layer.
conclusions: The first systematic analysis of this problem was conducted by Glorot and Bengio who showed that for a linear activation function, the optimal value of v^2 = 1/N, where N is the number of nodes feeding into that layer.

nodes.statement: Although the paper makes several assumptions about the inputs to the model, it works extremely well in many cases and is widely used in the initialization of neural networks to date; this initialization scheme is commonly referred to as the itXavier initialization.

nodes.statement: In an important follow up paper, He and colleagues argue that the itXavier initialization does not work well with the RELU activation function, and instead propose an initialization of v^2 = 2/N (commonly referred to as the itHe initialization).
